title: VPC isolation & egress probe / runtime latency deep dive
summary: Deep dive into Cobalt's private VPC deployment issues: recurring tail latency spikes observed in production during peak inference load. Focus areas: egress NAT hairpinning, PrivateLink routing, DNS timeouts, KV-cache warmup & eviction behavior, batching vs latency tradeoffs, and quantization impact. SE to reproduce with packet captures and eBPF; plan pilot with isolated subnet + modified NAT gateway rules.
topics: KV cache eviction patterns and prefix caching
dynamic batching thresholds and latency SLOs
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2027-10-25 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 min
- Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Lena (CSM), Marcus (Cobalt Platform), Anya (SRE), Darren (Security), Sofia (CTO - joined 00:18)

Auto-summary (auto): recurring tail-latency on Private VPC during 1k qps bursts; possible egress hairpin and DNS retry interplay; KV cache warmup not persistent across pods due to lifecycle.

[00:00] Jared: Hey folks, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you carving out time. Quick intro - I'm Jared, AE, with Priya who will run the tech bits.
[00:12] Priya: hi, hey. I'll jump straight in to what we saw in your perf logs that you shared. Marcus, do you want to confirm the spike windows again?
[00:20] Marcus: yeah, so around 11:30 UTC on Tuesday we saw token-level latency tail spike from median 120ms to 1.4s for about 7 minutes. CPU/GPU didn't show saturation, pods were healthy. We suspected network.
[00:35] Priya: ok. we pulled the request traces - there's a bunch of 5xx retries from the customer side and long DNS resolution steps in the trace. Also noticed multiple re-establish of KV cache - like cache misses right after pod restart.
[00:50] Anya: to be clear, we run two availability subnets, cross-account PrivateLink into Redwood Private - all traffic egresses via a NAT GW in account A. We do hairpinning (pod -> nat -> privatelink -> redwood) because our infra is, uh, locked down.
[01:10] Priya: hairpinning can add asymmetric pathing, and if MTU is mismatched you'll see fragmentation/retransmits which blow up tail latency. Did you have custom MTU on the transit VPC?
[01:20] Marcus: we have jumbo enabled for some subnets but the NAT GW is default 1500. Could be a mismatch. We haven't checked PMTU across the PrivateLink.
[01:32] Jared: also worth checking the PrivateLink health checks - some vendors use proxying which can add a hop. Darren, anything on security egress rules?
[01:40] Darren: we have strict egress e.g. TLS inspection from a proxy in account B for auditing. That proxy does SNI rewrite for certain domains, might be altering connection patterns. Not ideal but needed.
[01:52] Priya: SNI rewrite and a proxy that terminates TLS sometimes forces new connections and breaks keepalives; that will exacerbate KV cache cold starts because every new connection can create a new runtime view.
[02:05] Marcus: about KV cache - we run short lived pods for autoscale, so the model instance restart loses in-memory KV. But we expected prefix caching across pods via the shared cache layer; the logs show we aren't actually hitting that shared cache often.
[02:22] Priya: do you have sidecar or efs-based sharing?
[02:25] Marcus: no, it's ephemeral. We were hoping Redwood's platform could help with warmup + shared warm caches via prewarmed replicas.
[02:33] Priya: Redwood Dedicated supports persistent pre-warm pool, but in Private you control the infra. We can recommend a pre-warm daemonset that pins a small pool of model workers to avoid cold KV misses.
[02:46] Anya: that might work. But during the spike the DNS resolver in our VPC returned SERVFAIL for a subset of queries, then the client retried causing extra round trips.
[02:58] Priya: were you using an Amazon Route53 resolver ruleset or a custom in-VPC resolver?
[03:02] Marcus: custom - we run a DNS forwarding fleet (coreDNS) in each subnet. It forwards to the account-level resolver which then goes to Route53. We saw increased latency there.
[03:12] Priya: ok that chain + PrivateLink + proxying explains how a transient resolver blip turns into an application-level tail. Two recommendation areas: simplify the resolver chain (reduce hops) and exploit connection reuse to minimize DNS dependency per request.
[03:27] Jared: let's walk through a repro plan. Priya, can you outline the captures we need?
[03:32] Priya: sure. 1) tcpdump on the pod interface during a synthetic 1k qps test. 2) eBPF to capture socket lifetimes and retransmits. 3) collect CoreDNS logs and Route53 query metrics. 4) capture PrivateLink endpoint logs and NAT gateway flow logs.
[03:45] Anya: flow logs are heavy but ok for a short window. Darren: we might need to rotate keys for the proxy logs.
[03:52] Darren: noted. We'll give access via a pre-configured S3 bucket.
[03:58] [00:04:00] Marcus: Another angle - batching. We're using dynamic batching on the client side with target batch <8 tokens, but we still see per-request overhead. Could batching thresholds be causing delayed first token for short requests?
[04:12] Priya: yes, batching introduces queueing latency. The runtime has two knobs: max batch size and max batch wait (ms). If your SLO is P95 200ms, you might set max wait to 8-12ms and smaller batch sizes, or do adaptive batching with priority lanes for short latency-sensitive calls.
[04:30] Marcus: does Redwood runtime support warm prefix KVC sharing across concurrent model variants? We have some long context sessions that occasionally fallback to a smaller quantized model.
[04:40] Priya: we do prefix(KV) cache for active sessions, but cross-pod sharing needs a shared cache daemon. For fallbacks there's a cost: quantized model variant can change KV layout leading to cache invalidation. That may explain the warmup spikes when you switch variants.
[04:55] Anya: we do fallback to quantized 8-bit for low-priority workloads. Could that cause the 1.4s tail?
[04:58] Priya: potentially, especially if the quantized model forces dequantization steps that are single-threaded or not GPU-friendly on your instance type. Also some kernels for 8-bit have different attention memory patterns which can cause higher latency for long context.
[05:12] Sofia (CTO, joined): Sorry I'm late, quick context - we need sub-200ms P95 for our in-app assistant, anything above is customer-visible. We can't simply increase GPUs.
[05:22] Jared: understood. We'll aim for a mix of infra and runtime changes: network egress simplification, pre-warmed persistent workers, tuned batching, and targeted kernel selection/quantization profile review.
[05:32] Priya: let's go more granular on DNS interplay. In your traces I saw many tiny DNS lookups per request. Are you resolving a control plane endpoint per request?
[05:40] Marcus: our client libs instantiate a new HTTP client per invocation in some paths. Bad pattern, yes.
[05:46] Priya: that will trigger TLS handshakes and DNS lookups. Fixing the client to reuse a pool reduces 1) DNS load 2) TLS handshakes 3) KV cache churn due to connection affinity.
[05:58] Marcus: noted. We'll make that change and redeploy to staging.
[06:02] [00:06:12] Priya: on MTU - you mentioned jumbo frames enabled on some subnets. If the NAT or PrivateLink endpoint is 1500 and the path tries to send 9001 chunks you'll get fragmentation; path MTU discovery sometimes fails when ICMP blackhole is present. Do you block ICMP?
[06:15] Darren: our firewall historically blocks ICMP echo and some ICMP types. That could be the culprit.
[06:20] Priya: block ICMP leads to broken PMTU; packets get fragmented or retransmitted leading to big latency spikes. Recommend allow PMTU-related ICMP (Type 3 code 4) at minimum between subnets and the PrivateLink endpoint.
[06:32] Anya: we'll validate firewall rules.
[06:35] Jared: ok let's discuss KV cache eviction. Priya, you mentioned eviction due to memory pressure?
[06:40] Priya: right. If your pods are autoscaling aggressively and the model footprint is large, the OS might reclaim pages and the runtime will free KV. Two mitigations: 1) reserve memory on prewarmed pools, or 2) use pinned worker pool with fewer restarts. Also tune the runtime's eviction policy: prefer LRU at per-session granularity and increase hot-prefix retention windows.
[07:00] Marcus: how intrusive are those runtime config changes? Do we need a full upgrade?
[07:06] Priya: they are config flags in our Private runtime container; you can change them with a rollout and no model change. We'll prepare recommended flags.
[07:15] [00:07:20] Marcus: about NAT gateway - we use an autoscaling NAT fleet. Does NAT asymmetry matter for TLS?
[07:24] Priya: asymmetry per se isn't always a problem but if different egress IPs cause session affinity to break (e.g. firewall policies keyed off IP) then you'll see handshake repeats. Consistent egress IP or preserve source addresses helps.
[07:36] Darren: we do FB rules based on egress IP for some downstream services; that could be a source of churn.
[07:40] Priya: ok. Two short-term experiments: one, pin a small set of pods to a static NAT egress IP and run the synthetic load; two, run the same with coreDNS debug logging to reproduce the SERVFAILs.
[07:55] Anya: agreed. Also we want to test model quantization impact - is there a perf regression matrix?
[08:02] Priya: yes; we have a perf matrix that shows typical latency uplift for 8-bit qint vs fp16 on different sequence lengths and batch sizes. For short sequences (<64 tokens) 8-bit often wins for throughput but sometimes increases latency variance due to packing/unpacking overhead. We'll share the matrix and correlate with your seq length distribution.
[08:20] Marcus: sequence distribution is bimodal: 30% short chat (10-40 tokens), 60% medium (80-200), 10% long (400+).
[08:30] Priya: that explains why quantized fallback is hurting: those long contexts amplify the dequant overhead. Consider hybrid policy: use fp16 for long-context sessions and 8-bit for background batch jobs.
[08:44] Jared: let's capture the concrete next steps so Prod/SRE can action.
[08:48] [00:08:50] --- Quick recap by Jared ---
- Repro plan: synthetic 1k qps test with tcpdump + eBPF on pod interfaces; coreDNS logs + Route53 metrics; PrivateLink and NAT flow logs.
- Short-term fixes: allow PMTU ICMP types; pin egress IP for a small cohort; update client libs to reuse HTTP pools; deploy small prewarm pinned pool.
- Medium-term: review quantization policy per workload; tune kv-cache eviction windows; consider persistent shared cache daemon if autoscaling churn continues.

[00:09:40] Priya: I'll outline the tracer commands: tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap 'tcp and host <privatelink-ip>' and a bpftrace snippet to count retransmits and socket open/close. We'll attach the scripts to the follow-up doc.
[09:55] Marcus: great. For the prewarm pool, what's recommended size?
[09:58] Priya: start small: 3-5 pinned workers per AZ depending on your burst concurrency. If you're doing 1k qps with average 12 tokens per request, a 5 worker pool per AZ should absorb warmup. We'll run queuing-model calculations and share numbers.
[10:15] Anya: how about the fallback policy for quantized models — can Redwood do automatic routing to variant by prefix detection?
[10:22] Priya: yes, you can set routing by request characteristics; Redwood Console supports rollout rules: route long-context pinned sessions to fp16 variant while short sessions use quantized. But beware of cache invalidation on variant switch. Use sticky routing when possible.
[10:35] [00:10:40] Darren: security question - we need audit logs and KMS proofs for key material use if we store caches on shared storage. Is that supported?
[10:46] Priya: yes, Private deployments can integrate with your KMS/HSM; cache encryption at rest is supported and we can emit audit logs. We'll provide SOC2 artifact and KMS integration guide.
[10:58] Marcus: timeline - we want to run the reproduction in staging by 10/29 and have a mitigation plan by 11/02. Is that feasible?
[11:05] Priya: feasible. I can run the capture and initial analysis by 10/29, draft config changes 10/31.
[11:12] Jared: CSM Lena will coordinate schedules.
[11:15] Lena: I'll own scheduling + ensure access to flow logs and coreDNS bucket.
[11:20] [00:11:25] Priya: a few gotchas to watch: 1) client-side per-request DNS; 2) TLS-terminating proxies that re-negotiate every request; 3) cross-account PrivateLink endpoint misconfigs where IP translation creates extra hops.
[11:36] Marcus: noted. Also curious - would moving to Dedicated Reserved capacity remove some of these issues?
[11:42] Priya: Dedicated gives you predictable throughput and managed pre-warm pools, but it doesn't eliminate VPC-networking issues since egress and PrivateLink still exist. It just reduces model-level cold starts.
[11:54] Jared: quick Q from Darren - if we open ICMP for PMTU, what are the security implications?
[11:59] Darren: we can allow only specific ICMP codes between subnets and to PrivateLink endpoints. That's an acceptable risk if scoped properly.
[12:06] Priya: last technical note: enable per-route tracing on Redwood runtime to correlate request id -> socket lifecycle. That saved us in another deployment.
[12:14] Marcus: thanks.

[00:12:30] --- Late meeting wrap and next steps ---
[12:30] Jared: Ok action items and owners we will email. Any final questions?
[12:35] Sofia: thanks everyone. Keep it pragmatic - we need reproducible runs we can hand to infra on-call.
[12:40] Jared: will do. Thanks all.

End of transcript.
